items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: But then you’d go listen to Jimmy Blanton and he played great solos

ctx.x: Well one of the issues is when it gets to the bass solo then everybody just kinds of goes away and nobody’s listening. There’s so many jokes and I know you’ve heard them, you know, about to get people to start talking again just give them a bass solo. But the thing is that sometimes it’s nice. Like I have an album that’s coming out in the fall, and it’s a big band thing of mine, but I only have one solo. And it’s mine. It’s mine. Just because I’m the leader of a group doesn’t mean that I’m going to solo on…

you’ve been supporting all that. And then there’s nobody to support you when you play. And that can be a drag sometimes. And so we try to — well either I’m saying, well I don’t want to solo. Because sometimes the bass solo tanks that energy that has been already established. So I don’t want to do that too. If I’m going to do it, I want to help make it go too. So it’s a decision sometimes, and my ego — I like to solo, I want to solo, and I think I play better solos than I used to. But most people don’t hire me to…

Let’s talk about this conference we’re at. It’s an interesting state of affairs in jazz it seems like. If you come here — I just came from this little gathering of people talking about research. And in that room there was at least four or five different accents of people. In other words it was like an international group of people. And you’ve got I don’t know how many people here, and it makes jazz look really vibrant and healthy. And then you turn around and you read the typical “jazz is dead” article or — Gary…
